guide.achievements.p1: The Achievements tab tracks every trainer defeat, region clear and other milestones, alongside the household's current rarity bonus. Your own profile (click your name) shows your team, badges, champion titles, catch count, Pokédex progress and balance; co-players' profiles are visible read-only from the household bar. Pokédex achievements (seen all, caught all, living Pokédex) sit in their own group and make the Shiny Charm stronger or shinies more common; Pokémon of trainers you fight count as seen. Two more milestones reward raising your own Pokémon to level 100 - the 1st and the 10th ever (battle EXP, Rare Candy or Buddy walking all count, and releasing one later doesn't take the milestone away) each pay out an Exp. Share, a held item that gives its holder the same EXP as a fighting team member without joining the battle. More milestones pay out balls and Rare Candies: total catches (10 / 100 / 500 / 1000), 25 / 50 / 75% of the Pokédex caught, catching a roaming legendary (and all of them), and winning a daily challenge quest on 7 / 30 / 100 days in a row. Per generation (group "Generations", mythical Pokémon don't count): catching all of one pays ₽200,000 plus 40 Ultra Balls and makes that generation's wild Pokémon shiny 1.5× as often; owning all of one at once sends you every mythical Pokémon of that generation as an event encounter, and unlocks its sprite style, which you can set per Pokémon in its Pokédex entry.
guide.achievements.title: Achievements & profile
guide.auto_rules.p1: Auto rules (Settings → Auto rules) handle wild Pokémon for you. Each rule has conditions (IF: level, generation, rarity, type, shiny, Pokédex and IV progress, catch chance, where it spawned, your team's state …) and an action (THEN: beat it, catch it, throw balls without a battle, let it go, or leave it to you). For each encounter the first active rule from the top whose conditions all match decides.
guide.auto_rules.p2: Catching weakens the Pokémon with moves that won't knock it out and throws once your chosen ball reaches the catch chance you set – it can pick the cheapest ball that is good enough, re-buy balls within a money reserve and your daily budget, heal your team first and send catches to the box. Shiny, legendary and mythical Pokémon are never let go and the Master Ball is never thrown unless a rule explicitly allows it.
guide.auto_rules.p3: Rules run when you press “Run rules” in the queue, and – if you switch it on – automatically as soon as a Pokémon spawns. The household's auto-battle switch (admin) must be on. “Test against my queue” shows what would happen without changing anything, and the history marks every battle a rule fought.
guide.auto_rules.title: Auto rules
guide.battle_style.p1: In gym, league and player battles, your battle style decides what happens once a trainer's Pokémon faints (except the very last one): with the default “Set” style their next Pokémon comes straight out and the fight continues, with “Shift” you get a free switch first – or just pick a move to decline it. Change it anytime under Settings → Gameplay; a battle already in progress keeps the style it started with. Wild battles always play like Set.
guide.battle_style.title: Battle style
guide.breeding.p1: The Day Care (Team tab) takes two compatible Pokémon – male + female sharing an Egg Group, or either one paired with Ditto – and produces an Egg from time to time, without removing either parent from use.
guide.breeding.p2: An Egg hatches after enough steps, counted only while it sits in your team or in an Incubator. Steps come from your step sensor (the same one used for your Buddy Pokémon) plus a small passive trickle even without one.
guide.breeding.title: Breeding
guide.buddy.p1: Pick one of your Pokémon as your buddy (Team tab → Buddy, or the “Make buddy” button in a Pokémon's detail view). The add-on mirrors it into Home Assistant as a sensor named after your HA username (e.g. sensor.pokemon_buddy_alice): the state is the level, the picture is the Pokémon's sprite, and attributes carry its name, types, official artwork and walking progress. Add it to a dashboard with a tile, picture-entity or markdown card – ready-made examples are in the add-on documentation.
guide.buddy.p2: Choose a step or distance sensor from Home Assistant (for example the Companion App's step sensor) in the Buddy view. Every 6500 steps you walk (about 5 km / 3 mi; the household can change this in Settings) give your buddy +1 level, like a Rare Candy (max. level 100; evolutions stay manual). Distance sensors work too – they are converted to steps. The first reading after choosing a sensor is only the starting point, a counter reset at midnight is handled automatically, and absurd jumps are ignored.
guide.buddy.p3: The same step sensor also hatches your Eggs. Steps you have banked belong to the current buddy and are lost when you switch. Your buddy can't be traded. The sensor refreshes with every poll and immediately when you change your buddy; after a Home Assistant restart it is missing until the next poll.
guide.buddy.title: Buddy & Home Assistant
guide.catching.p1: You don't have to attack first – a ball can fly on your very first turn. Catch chance mainly depends on the wild Pokémon's remaining HP and its base catch rate, so weakening it (without knocking it out) before throwing usually pays off. A failed throw costs the ball and gives the wild Pokémon another turn; a status condition like sleep or paralysis helps too. Watch out: a wild Pokémon that has leveled up during the current battle can no longer be caught in that battle.
guide.catching.p2: Poké Ball, Great Ball and Ultra Ball simply add a flat multiplier. The special balls from the main series are situational instead – Timer Ball rewards a long fight, Quick Ball rewards throwing right at the start, Dusk Ball wants nighttime, Fast Ball wants a high-Speed target, and so on; the Shop and Bag mark whichever one is currently boosted with a ★ and its multiplier. Master Ball always catches but can't be bought.
guide.catching.p3: Pokédex progress (more species caught) slowly raises the chance of a critical catch – a single, near-guaranteed shake instead of the usual up to four.
guide.catching.title: Catching
guide.evolution.p1: Level evolutions don't happen automatically: once a Pokémon reaches the required level, an “Evolve” button appears for it in the Team tab. Other evolutions need an item (evolution stone, Link Cable, …) bought in the Shop and used from the Bag.
guide.evolution.title: Evolution
guide.evs.p1: Besides its randomly rolled IVs, every Pokémon has six Effort Values – EVs for short – that you set yourself: training points on a single stat. Every 4 EVs in a stat are worth one more point of it at level 100 (half that at level 50), so a fully trained stat ends up 63 points higher.
guide.evs.p2: EVs come from two places. Every species has an EV yield (taken from the PokeAPI – Pikachu gives 2 Speed, Geodude 1 Defense, and so on): each of your Pokémon that took part in a wild, gym or league battle and was still standing when an opponent fell gets that opponent's yield – it keeps them even if it faints later or the whole battle is lost. The battle log shows what it gained. Catches and player battles give no EVs. On top of that, a vitamin (HP Up, Protein, Iron, Calcium, Zinc, Carbos) gives +10 EVs on its stat, a wing +1 for fine-tuning, and a berry (Pomeg, Kelpsy, Qualot, Hondew, Grepa, Tamato) takes 10 back off if you invested in the wrong place. Buy them in the Shop and use them in the Bag on any of your Pokémon – no fighting required.
guide.evs.p3: Limits are the same as in the main games: at most 252 EVs in a single stat and 510 in total, so you can max out two stats and spread the rest. The Pokémon's detail view shows its EVs, what they're worth and how much of the budget is left. EVs belong to the Pokémon: they survive evolution and trades, and your team fights player battles with them.
guide.evs.title: EVs (Effort Values)
guide.gym_difficulty.p1: Under Settings → Gameplay you can restrict gym and league battles further: with the default difficulty your whole team fights, capped to the trainer's level as always. With “Generation limit” only Pokémon from the trainer's own generation or exactly one generation older are allowed to fight at all – anything younger or more than one generation older sits that particular battle out. “Same generation” is stricter still: only Pokémon from exactly the trainer's (the league's) own generation may fight, no generation older allowed either. Either way, the Gyms & League tab marks trainers your whole team is currently ineligible for. Change it anytime; a battle already in progress keeps the difficulty it started with.
guide.gym_difficulty.title: Gym difficulty
guide.healing.p1: Outside of battle every Pokémon slowly regenerates HP over time, even fainted ones, and “Heal team” (Team tab) tops off your whole team at once before going on cooldown for a while. Beating an Elite Four member speeds up regeneration a little and shortens that cooldown; beating a Champion shortens it further still.
guide.healing.p2: “Auto heal” (turn it on under Settings → Gameplay, then use the button in the Team tab) heals your whole team from the Bag with the cheapest combination of potions that covers each Pokémon's missing HP, skipping fainted Pokémon and anything your stock can't fully cover. “Auto buy used potions” restocks exactly what Auto heal just spent, as far as your money reaches.
guide.healing.title: Healing
guide.intro: A quick rundown of every system running in the background – spawns, catching, IVs, evolution and more. Nothing here is required reading, but it explains the numbers you see elsewhere in the app.
guide.items.p1: Held items (Team tab) sit on a Pokémon and act passively in battle – Leftovers heals a little each turn, Choice Band boosts Attack but locks the move, a Sitrus Berry is consumed once it triggers, and so on.
guide.items.p2: Medicine (Bag tab, or the Bag action in battle) heals HP and cures status conditions – potions, full heals, revives for fainted Pokémon. Using an item on a battle turn costs that turn, same as attacking.
guide.items.title: Held items & medicine
guide.ivs.p1: Like in the main games, every Pokémon secretly rolls six Individual Values (HP, Attack, Defense, Sp. Atk, Sp. Def, Speed, each 0–31) the moment it's caught or hatched. They're fixed for that Pokémon's life and quietly push its stats up or down compared to another of the same species and level – shown as small bars in its detail view.
guide.ivs.p2: Catching a species you already own a family member of (same evolution line) raises one random, not-yet-maxed IV of each existing family member by a point or two – a small, permanent reward for catching duplicates instead of releasing them.
guide.ivs.p3: Every catch of a species also permanently raises the household's IV floor for that species by a point on a random stat – new spawns of it can never roll below that floor. Catch enough of one species and every future spawn of it will have perfect IVs.
guide.ivs.title: IVs (Individual Values)
guide.leveling.p1: Pokémon gain EXP for every opponent Pokémon defeated in wild battles, gym/league battles and auto-battle – even fainted teammates and losing battles still grant EXP. Level-ups happen automatically once enough EXP is collected.
guide.leveling.p2: A Rare Candy instantly grants one level to a Pokémon of your choice, no battle needed. Buy it in the Shop, or release a Pokémon from your box (Team tab) – it rewards Rare Candy instead of just vanishing.
guide.leveling.title: Levels, EXP & Rare Candy
guide.mega.p1: A Mega stone is a held item made for exactly one species – give a Charizard its Charizardite X and it can Mega Evolve. You buy the stones in the shop ("Mega stones") and equip them in the Team tab, just like any other held item.
guide.mega.p2: In battle a button above your moves offers the Mega Evolution. It is free – it does not cost your turn – but only one Pokémon per side and battle can use it. The form lasts until the battle ends and brings new base stats, sometimes a new type and always a new ability; afterwards your Pokémon is exactly as it was, nothing changes permanently. Kyogre and Groudon use the Blue and Red Orb the same way for their Primal forms.
guide.mega.title: Mega Evolution
guide.pvp.p1: Challenging another household member never touches their real team: you fight an AI-controlled snapshot of it, taken the moment the battle starts. Your own team can take damage during the fight but is always fully healed afterwards, win or lose – it's sparring, not a real encounter.
guide.pvp.p2: Your profile also generates a short team code others can enter to preview and battle a copy of your team, even outside the household – handy for sharing a team without a live connection.
guide.pvp.title: Player battles & team codes
guide.regions.p1: Every region's gym leaders, Elite Four and champion can be challenged at any time from the Gyms & League tab; your Pokémon fight capped to the opponent's highest level if they're stronger, so overleveling can't trivialize a league. EXP is awarded for every defeated opponent Pokémon regardless of outcome.
guide.regions.p2: What a cleared league does for your wild spawn pool depends on your region lock (chosen when you pick your starter, changeable later in Settings → Gameplay). With the default “Region” lock, defeating every trainer of a region unlocks that generation's Pokémon in your own wild spawn pool (Kanto/Generation 1 is open from the very start). League progress and the unlock are both per player – another player clearing a league does nothing for your spawns.
guide.regions.p3: Beating every trainer in every region awards the “League Champion” achievement and a Shiny Charm.
guide.regions.p4: The three region locks: “Unlocked” – every generation spawns from the very start, clearing leagues only earns rewards and rarer spawns. “Region” – clearing a region unlocks that region's own generation (Johto → Gen 2, Hoenn → Gen 3, …). “Progression” – clearing a region unlocks the NEXT generation (Kanto → Gen 2, Johto → Gen 3, …), so you always meet the next generation's Pokémon before you face its league. Switching the lock later never takes anything away that you already caught; it only changes what can spawn for you.
guide.regions.title: Regions & the League
guide.shiny.p1: Every spawn has a small, independent chance (1 in 4096, like in recent main games) to be shiny – a purely cosmetic recolor with a sparkle in the log and its own sprite. Owning a Shiny Charm doubles that chance for your own spawns and Eggs.
guide.shiny.title: Shiny Pokémon
guide.spawns.p1: Every configured Home Assistant entity (motion sensor, light switch, zone, …) can spawn a wild Pokémon when it changes state – into your own queue: one trigger creates one encounter per player, each rolled separately, so what you get is independent of everyone else. Unhandled encounters flee after a few days (see Settings).
guide.spawns.p2: Which species shows up depends on its rarity tier (common, rare, pseudo-legendary, paradox, legendary, mythical), the triggering entity's type bonus (a light switch favors Electric types, for example) and, for outdoor triggers like zones or device trackers, the biome of that location (forest, cave, beach, …). Only base forms spawn in the wild – evolutions come from leveling up or evolution items.
guide.spawns.p3: Fully clearing a region's league (see “Regions & the League” below) permanently shifts YOUR odds toward rarer tiers – mythical Pokémon become far more common once you've beaten every region.
guide.spawns.title: Encounters & the queue
guide.title: How the game works
guide.tms.p1: Every gym leader hands out a TM the first time you beat them – the same one they do in the main games, wherever that move exists here. A TM is the only way around the normal learnset: it teaches its move to a compatible Pokémon, off-type included, as soon as that Pokémon reaches the move's level. Which Pokémon can learn a TM follows the main games (data from PokéAPI): Blastoise can learn Ice Beam, Magikarp learns none. A few TMs use moves that are no TM in the main games; for those, types and attack stats decide. Teaching uses the TM up, so a TM several regions award (Rock Tomb) is worth beating each of those gyms for.
guide.tms.p2: Apply a TM in the Bag tab, then pick which of your four battle moves it replaces in the Team tab (a free slot is filled right away). Badges also pay out balls – from 2 Poké Balls for a region's first gym up to 5 Poké, 5 Great and 5 Ultra Balls for its eighth – and clearing a whole region earns one Master Ball.
guide.tms.title: TMs & gym rewards
guide.trade.p1: Trade Pokémon with another household member in the Trading tab: pick a player and one of your box Pokémon and send the request. The other player accepts it by offering one of their own Pokémon (or refuses). You then see the final offer and decide – only when you accept, both Pokémon swap owners, otherwise nothing changes.
guide.trade.p2: Only Pokémon in the box can be traded – not team members, your buddy or day care parents. Level, IVs, nature, ability, TMs and the held item go along; the new owner's Pokédex counts it as caught. Finished trades can be removed from your view and disappear on their own the next day.
guide.trade.title: Trading
guide.typechart.p1: Find the type of the move in the left column and the type of the target in the top row. A green 2 means super effective (double damage), an orange ½ means not very effective (half damage), a grey 0 means no effect at all. Empty cells are neutral.
guide.typechart.p2: Pokémon with two types multiply both values: a Fire move against Grass/Steel is 2 × 2 = 4× damage, while Ground against Flying does nothing whatever the second type is. Some abilities (like Levitate) add immunities on top of this chart.
guide.typechart.title: Type chart

tutorial.catching_text: Example: a wild Pidgey shows up in your queue. You open it, throw a Poké Ball and try to catch it – the lower its HP and the better your ball, the higher your chance. If it breaks free, it just gets another turn and you can try again.
tutorial.healing_text: Pokémon slowly heal on their own over time. You can also use a Potion from your Bag, or press “Heal team” in the Team tab to top everyone off at once. Other items in the Bag and Shop help with evolving, boost your Pokémon in battle, and more.
